method_note: FAST mode, one round. F-001 to F-019 reused from articles/2026-11-17-bali-wedding-packages/02-research-B.json, keeping original checked dates; source_ref gives the original ID. New facts from F-100.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia: 'Generally, Indonesian nationals, and persons of any other nationality may marry in Indonesia provided they hold a religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism or Christian). Under the Indonesian Marriage Law, marriages may be performed by Ministers of Religion, officers of the Civil Registry Office (Kantor Catatan Sipil) or the Office of Religious Affairs (Kantor Urusan Agama). For a marriage to be legal, it must be conducted according to the religion and conform to the laws of the countries of the parties involved.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Quote as the Embassy's 'general guide only'. The religion list is the Embassy's short form; see new facts for the Indonesian official position. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage takes place, or the Indonesian Embassy or Consulate-General in Australia.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, 'Couples must be of the same religion': 'Under Indonesian Law No.1 of 1974 concerning marriage (the 'Marriage Law'), both parties must hold the same religion, if not, one party must convert to the other religion.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: This is the Embassy's reading of the law; the statute itself does not use the words 'same religion' (see F-1xx on art. 2(1)). Quote it as the Embassy's wording. Do not repeat the Embassy's 'anecdotal' remark about conversion. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office and the Australian Consulate-General Bali.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, Other Weddings: for non-Muslim marriages (Christian, Hindu, etc.), couples lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding; after the ceremony the marriage must be registered at the Civil Registry Office to be legal. Both applicants need originals and photocopies of: the CNI from the Embassy or Consulate-General; passports or KTP; birth certificates; marriage certificate; proof of dissolution of a previous marriage or death certificate of a former partner (if applicable); four photos (4x6cm) of the couple. Requirements can vary from province to province, so check with the Civil Registry Office where you will marry first.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: 'Marriage certificate' appears in the list as written; its meaning is unclear (likely the religious certificate), so say 'the documents your Civil Registry Office lists'. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office (Dinas Kependudukan dan Pencatatan Sipil) of the regency where you marry.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, Islamic Weddings: Muslim weddings are performed by the Office of Religious Affairs (Kantor Urusan Agama), which issues the Marriage Book (Buku Nikah) as evidence of the marriage. There is usually no requirement to register such a marriage with the Civil Registry Office, but a Civil Registry Marriage Certificate is recommended if you intend to relocate to another country.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia

facts.claim: Indonesia (including Bali): an Australian marrying in Indonesia applies for a Certificate of No Impediment (CNI) from the Australian Embassy in Jakarta or a Consulate-General; Bali, NTB and NTT fall under the Australian Consulate-General in Bali. The local Civil Registry Office or KUA normally requires the CNI from the mission with jurisdiction.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Confirmed by the Australian Consulate-General Bali and the Civil Registry Office where the marriage will take place.

facts.claim: Indonesia: 'We do not place an expiry date on the CNI, however the local Civil Registry Office do not normally accept CNIs that were issued more than 3 months prior.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Civil Registry practice, not law; confirm with the Civil Registry Office in the regency where you marry.

facts.claim: Indonesia: for non-Muslim marriages, couples lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding, and the marriage must be registered there afterwards to be legal. Both parties must hold the same religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (Law No. 1 of 1974). A CNI is usually issued while you wait if documents are complete.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: The Embassy calls this 'a general guide only'. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office in the area of the wedding.

facts.claim: Indonesia: Government Regulation (PP) No. 9 of 1975, implementing Marriage Law No. 1 of 1974, article 10: following the procedure of each religion or belief, the marriage takes place before the Registrar (Pegawai Pencatat) and is attended by two witnesses ('dihadiri oleh dua orang saksi').
facts.publisher: Badan Pemeriksa Keuangan RI (Indonesian Audit Board) legal database
facts.use_note: Medium: confirmed via search excerpts, not read in full. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office in Bali.
